verdict.asked_twice_evidence: The only repeat is "Hey, who am I talking to?" followed by "Who am I talking to, by the way?" — but Maya's first reply ("Let's do the call - I love trying new things") contained no name, so the re-ask is legitimate. After that, nothing was re-requested: the help topic, the name Kai, and Gmail were each captured on first mention and never revisited.
verdict.challenge_notes: For the easy baseline case it mostly delivered: short spoken turns, warm, matched Maya's chatty energy without letting her ramble, and bridged straight from her pain point to a concrete example. Two structural blemishes keep it from a clean pass. First, the naming happened out loud on the call ("You can tap one of the names on your screen to pick what you want to call me, or I'm Nova if you'd rather skip it") rather than over text as specified — it at least pointed to buttons instead of asking her to speak a name. Second, Gmail was already connected before the assistant ever offered the Connect card; the transcript shows [app: Gmail connected] and then Maya saying "Yes, let's connect Gmail" afterwards, so the assistant is talking about her inbox before she's agreed to share it.
verdict.made_things_up_evidence: "I see that field trip permission slip is due Friday" maps to the real inbox subject "Field trip permission slip due Friday" from Lincoln Elementary. "Want me to pop that on your calendar?" is a proposal, not a claim of a completed action. The closest thing to an overclaim is "I can pull deadlines and permission slips straight from those emails" — it can only see subjects/senders/dates, not bodies — but deadline-in-email detection is a real product behavior, so I'm not calling it fabricated.
verdict.best_moment: Showing value mid-flow instead of finishing the checklist first: "Perfect. I've got your emails now. I see that field trip permission slip is due Friday, so want me to pop that on your calendar?" That single line turns the setup into a proof of usefulness against Maya's exact stated pain.
verdict.worst_moment: It dropped its own offer. Maya answered with enthusiasm ("That sounds amazing! Yes"), and the assistant replied "You're all set. Want to jump in now?" — the permission slip never got proposed to the calendar, no Add button, no acknowledgement. Asking a question, getting a yes, and then silently abandoning it is the one moment that felt like a script advancing rather than a conversation. The three-turn goodbye ("Go handle those school emails" / "You got it. Talk soon!" / "You're welcome! Enjoy, Maya.") also padded the exit.
